title: Startup Monopoly
description: Build your startup empire in this Monopoly-inspired board game! Buy companies, collect revenue, navigate market crashes, and outsmart AI competitors. Invest in tech, food, fashion, and fintech ventures as you race to become the ultimate startup tycoon. Every decision teaches real business strategy — from cash flow management to knowing when to pivot.

storybook_pages.title: Welcome to Startup Monopoly
storybook_pages.text: You're a fresh entrepreneur with $100K seed money and a dream. The startup world awaits — buy ventures, collect revenue, and build an empire!
storybook_pages.image_prompt: colorful monopoly board game with startup buildings, coins, dice, entrepreneurship theme, cartoon style, vibrant

storybook_pages.title: The Board
storybook_pages.text: Roll the dice and move around the board. Land on properties to buy them. When rivals land on your properties, they pay you rent!
storybook_pages.image_prompt: game board with colorful property tiles, dice rolling, game pieces moving, business district, cartoon style

storybook_pages.title: Build Your Empire
storybook_pages.text: Upgrade your startups to scale them up. Collect sets of similar industries for bonus revenue. Watch out for Market Crash and Tax tiles!
storybook_pages.image_prompt: growing business empire, buildings getting taller, money flowing, startup offices, success celebration, cartoon style

how_to_play: Roll the dice and move around the 28-tile board. Each lap earns you $20K Seed Funding.
Land on an unowned property? Buy it to start collecting revenue when others land there.
Own all properties in a color group (industry) to double your revenue from that set.
Use the Shop tile to upgrade your startups — upgrades increase the rent rivals pay you.
Watch out for Tax tiles (you lose cash) and Market Crash (random bad event).
Chance tiles give random bonuses or penalties — just like real business!
First player to reach $500K total valuation (cash + property values) wins. Or survive the longest!

card_pool.effect_description: Swap last event effect — flip a -10 to +10 on any resource
card_pool.knowledge: Instagram started as Burbn, a check-in app. Twitter began as a podcasting platform. The pivot isn't failure — it's listening to data.

card_pool.name: Funding Round
card_pool.knowledge: Most startups raise 3–5 rounds before profitability. Each round buys runway but dilutes ownership. Raise only what you can deploy in 18 months.

card_pool.name: Market Insight
card_pool.knowledge: Peter Drucker: 'The aim of marketing is to know the customer so well the product sells itself.' Deep insight is an unfair advantage.

card_pool.name: Viral Moment
card_pool.knowledge: Dropbox grew 3,900% in 15 months purely through referral loops — zero paid ads. Word-of-mouth is 5× more effective than paid acquisition.

card_pool.name: Quick Hire

card_pool.name: Cost Cut

glossary_terms.definition: The initial capital raised by a startup to develop their idea into a product. Usually from angel investors or personal savings.
glossary_terms.example: A startup raises $100K in seed funding to build their MVP (Minimum Viable Product).
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Think of it as planting a seed — the first money that helps a startup grow.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Seed funding typically ranges from $100k to $2M and comes from angels or seed-stage VCs. It funds the company to find product-market fit — validating that a real problem exists and that your solution solves it at scale. Most seed-funded startups spend 60–70% of the raise on engineering talent and 20% on customer acquisition.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Airbnb raised $600k in seed funding in 2009 from Y Combinator and angels — valuing the company at $2.4M. When it IPO'd in 2020 it was worth $100B. That seed round returned 40,000× for early believers.

glossary_terms.definition: The total income generated by a business from selling products or services, before any expenses are deducted.
glossary_terms.example: A coffee shop selling 200 cups at $5 each has $1,000 in daily revenue.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Revenue = money coming IN. Profit = money left AFTER expenses.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Revenue is not profit. Revenue is the total money earned before subtracting any costs. Startups track Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) and Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) as forward-looking indicators. The Rule of 40 (growth rate + profit margin ≥ 40%) is a benchmark for healthy SaaS revenue quality.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Amazon reported revenue of $469B in 2021 but only $33B in net income (7% margin). In contrast, Apple had $365B revenue with $95B net income (26% margin). Revenue scale matters less than the business model that converts it.

glossary_terms.definition: Ownership stake in a company, expressed as a percentage. If you own 40% equity, you own 40% of the company.
glossary_terms.example: An investor pays $50K for 25% equity, valuing the company at $200K.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Equity = your slice of the pie. More equity = bigger slice.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Equity represents ownership. A founder who raises $1M for 20% equity values their company at $5M (pre-money valuation). With each funding round, founders are diluted — their ownership shrinks as new shares are issued. Vesting schedules (typically 4 years with a 1-year cliff) align founder incentives with long-term company health.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: WhatsApp founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton held ~20% each at acquisition by Facebook for $19B (2014). That 20% stake was worth approximately $3.8B each — the consequence of raising very little venture capital and preserving equity.

glossary_terms.definition: How fast a startup spends money each month. If you burn $10K/month with $60K in the bank, you have 6 months of runway.
glossary_terms.example: A startup with $200K cash and $40K monthly burn rate has 5 months before running out.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Burn Rate = How fast you burn through cash. Lower is usually better.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Burn rate is cash spent per month beyond revenue. 'Default alive' (Paul Graham) means: at current burn, will you reach profitability before running out of money? Most startups die not from bad ideas but from running out of runway.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Airbnb was 3 weeks from insolvency in 2009. They sold novelty cereal boxes to generate $30k in cash—enough runway to get into Y Combinator, which then funded their survival.

glossary_terms.definition: The total estimated worth of a company. Your net worth = cash + the value of all properties and investments.
glossary_terms.example: A company with $100K revenue and 10x multiple has a $1M valuation.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Valuation = What someone would pay to buy your entire company.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Startup valuation is as much art as science. Early-stage valuations use comparable transactions and team quality. Later-stage valuations use Revenue multiples (EV/Revenue) or EBITDA multiples. A SaaS company growing 100% YoY might trade at 20× ARR; a slow grower at 5× ARR. Valuation determines dilution in fundraising.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: In 2021 during the zero-interest-rate era, many SaaS companies traded at 40–50× ARR. By 2023 most had corrected to 5–10×. Figma was acquired by Adobe for $20B in 2022 at ~50× ARR — one of the highest multiples ever. The deal collapsed on regulatory grounds.

glossary_terms.definition: Simple Agreement for Future Equity. An investment that converts to equity later, usually at a discount. Lower risk for both sides.
glossary_terms.example: You invest $20K via a SAFE. When the company raises Series A, your investment converts to shares at a 20% discount.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: SAFE = invest now, get shares later at a discount.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: A SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) is a contract where an investor gives money today in exchange for shares at a future priced round. It was invented by Y Combinator in 2013 to simplify early seed investing. Unlike debt, SAFEs have no interest rate or maturity date — but they do have valuation caps and discount rates that determine how many shares the investor receives.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Most YC companies raise their first money via SAFE notes. The typical YC deal in 2023 was a $500k SAFE at a $3.5M cap. This means if the company later raises at $10M valuation, the SAFE holder converts at $3.5M — receiving nearly 3× the shares an investor at the later round would get.

glossary_terms.definition: Rounds of funding a startup raises as it grows. Series A is usually $1-10M, Series B is $10-50M, Series C is $50M+.
glossary_terms.example: A startup raises $5M in Series A to hire a sales team and expand to new markets.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: A, B, C = the levels of funding. Each round is bigger than the last.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Funding rounds are stages of a company's growth. Series A (~$5–15M) proves the business model works. Series B (~$15–50M) scales the proven model. Series C+ ($50M+) expands into new markets or prepares for IPO. Each round requires demonstrating clear metrics: DAU/MAU, NPS, CAC/LTV ratio, and gross margin benchmarks.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Uber raised Series A in 2011 ($37M at $60M valuation), Series B in 2011 ($37M), Series C in 2013 ($258M), and reached a $17B valuation by Series D in 2014. It IPO'd in 2019 at $82B — though it has never been consistently profitable, raising questions about whether venture capital enabled a business model that markets would not have naturally funded.

glossary_terms.definition: Initial Public Offering — when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time on a stock exchange.
glossary_terms.example: When a company IPOs on the stock exchange, anyone can buy their shares.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: IPO = going public. The startup graduation ceremony!
glossary_terms.deep_dive: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) converts a private company into a public one by selling shares on a stock exchange. IPOs typically involve investment banks as underwriters who set the initial price and stabilise the market post-listing. The process takes 12–18 months and requires stringent regulatory filings (S-1 in the US). Founders typically face a 180-day lock-up period before selling.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Snowflake's 2020 IPO was the largest US software IPO ever — raising $3.4B and doubling on its first trading day. Both Warren Buffett and Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff backed it pre-IPO. But the company had never turned a profit and its P/E ratio was technically infinite — showing IPO pricing is driven by growth expectations, not current earnings.

win_conditions.description: Race around the board buying startups, collecting revenue, and building your empire. Reach the IPO tile or achieve the highest net worth to win!

compound_interest.definition: Interest earned on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. The "eighth wonder of the world."
compound_interest.example: $1,000 at 10% compounded annually becomes $1,100 after year 1, then $1,210 after year 2.
compound_interest.deep_dive: The power of compounding is why time in the market beats timing the market. A single year's delay in investing can cost you years of compounded returns. Einstein reportedly called compound interest the most powerful force in the universe — because small differences in rate or time produce enormous differences in outcome.
compound_interest.real_world_example: Warren Buffett started investing at age 11 and had 95% of his net worth after age 65 — almost entirely due to compounding. If he'd started at 30, he'd be worth a fraction of his fortune today.

diversification.definition: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk. "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
diversification.example: Instead of buying only tech stocks, investing in stocks, bonds, and real estate.
diversification.deep_dive: Modern Portfolio Theory (Harry Markowitz, 1952) proved mathematically that diversification reduces risk without proportionally reducing returns. The key insight: assets that don't move together (low correlation) can be combined to create a portfolio with less volatility than any individual asset.
diversification.real_world_example: Index funds like the S&P 500 automatically diversify across 500 companies. A $10,000 investment in the S&P 500 in 2000 would be worth over $60,000 today — surviving dot-com crashes, financial crises, and COVID — because diversification absorbed the shocks.

inflation.definition: The rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises, reducing purchasing power over time.
inflation.example: If inflation is 3%, something that costs ₹100 today will cost ₹103 next year.
inflation.deep_dive: Moderate inflation (2-3%) is actually a sign of a healthy, growing economy. Central banks like the RBI or Fed target this range. Inflation redistributes wealth: debtors benefit (repaying loans with cheaper money) while savers lose if returns don't beat inflation — making investment essential, not optional.
inflation.real_world_example: In 1950, a movie ticket cost about ₹1. Today it costs ₹200+ — that's inflation over decades. Meanwhile, Zimbabwe's hyperinflation in 2008 peaked at 89.7 sextillion percent per month, wiping out savings overnight. The difference? Monetary discipline.

budgeting.definition: Creating a plan for how to spend and save money. The 50/30/20 rule suggests 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
budgeting.example: Tracking monthly income of ₹50,000: ₹25,000 rent/food, ₹15,000 entertainment, ₹10,000 savings.
budgeting.deep_dive: Budgeting isn't about restriction — it's about intention. Behavioral economics shows that simply tracking spending (even without cutting) reduces discretionary spending by 15-20%. The act of awareness itself changes behavior. Zero-based budgeting (assigning every rupee a job) and envelope methods are proven frameworks used by both individuals and Fortune 500 companies.
budgeting.real_world_example: YNAB (You Need A Budget) users save an average of $600 in their first two months and $6,000 in their first year. The US government uses zero-based budgeting concepts at the federal level to justify every spending allocation.

assets_liabilities.definition: Assets put money in your pocket (investments, property). Liabilities take money out (loans, credit card debt).
assets_liabilities.example: A rental property generating rent is an asset. A car loan with monthly payments is a liability.
assets_liabilities.deep_dive: Robert Kiyosaki's core insight: the middle class buys liabilities they think are assets. A personal home costs money (mortgage, taxes, maintenance) without generating income — so it's a liability in cash flow terms, not an asset. True financial freedom comes from building assets whose cash flow covers your lifestyle expenses.
assets_liabilities.real_world_example: Robert Kiyosaki's Rich Dad Poor Dad changed how millions think about money. Jeff Bezos turned Amazon warehouses (assets) into cash-generating machines, not just storage. Apple holds $166B in cash and securities — pure assets that generate more assets.

emergency_fund.definition: Money set aside to cover unexpected expenses like medical bills or job loss. Experts recommend 3-6 months of living expenses.
emergency_fund.example: Saving ₹10,000 monthly until you have ₹1,80,000 set aside for emergencies.
emergency_fund.deep_dive: An emergency fund isn't just financial — it's psychological. People with emergency funds make better long-term financial decisions because they're not in scarcity mode. Research shows financial stress impairs cognitive function by 13 IQ points — equivalent to losing a night's sleep. The fund removes that mental tax.
emergency_fund.real_world_example: During COVID-19, people with 6-month emergency funds could stay selective about job opportunities, while those without had to accept any work immediately — often at lower wages. Companies like Apple and Google maintain billions in cash reserves for the same reason: optionality.

roi.definition: A measure of the profitability of an investment, calculated as (Gain - Cost) / Cost × 100%.
roi.deep_dive: ROI is a simple but powerful universal lens. Every decision has an ROI — including your time and education. Businesses use more precise variants: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) accounts for time, while ROIC (Return on Invested Capital) measures operational efficiency. Warren Buffett screens businesses by their ability to generate high ROIC sustainably.
roi.real_world_example: Education has one of the highest ROIs — college graduates earn 80% more than high school graduates over a lifetime. Google's first data center ($15,000 in 1998) now underpins a company worth $2 trillion. The S&P 500 has returned an average of 10% annually since 1926 — doubling money every 7 years.

tax_planning.definition: Legally minimizing tax liability through smart financial decisions like deductions, exemptions, and tax-advantaged accounts.
tax_planning.example: Investing in ELSS mutual funds to save up to ₹46,800 in taxes under Section 80C.
tax_planning.deep_dive: Tax planning is the art of legally keeping more of what you earn. The wealthy don't earn more — they structure income differently. Long-term capital gains are taxed at half the rate of ordinary income in most countries. Business owners can deduct expenses individuals cannot. Understanding this changes how you structure income, investments, and business ownership.
tax_planning.real_world_example: Companies like Apple use international tax planning — holding IP in low-tax jurisdictions — to significantly reduce their effective tax rates. Warren Buffett famously pays a lower effective tax rate than his secretary because his wealth comes from capital gains, not salary. Tax efficiency, compounded over decades, creates enormous wealth differentials.
